meta.q:
Concrete engineering review, answer in English.

Context: a Minecraft AI companion is supervised by a separate "planner"

text:
1) Is 5s right? No — it’s below the minimum of your own latency distribution

First, establish what the timer actually measures. Tool calls only happen when a response arrives, so “zero tool calls for 5s” ≈ “current request has been in flight for 5s.” Compare against your samples:

Threshold	Fires on (in-flight)	True stalls among firings	Precision
5s	5.5, 6.5, 14.3, 35.6, 44.0 → all 5	0 during flight*	~0
15s (old)	35.6, 44.0	0 during flight*	~0
any T	—	—	—

*Key point: a nudge fired mid-flight cannot reach the model. The request is already sent; the nudge queues for the next turn. So for the 35.6s idle case, nudges at 5/10/15/…/30s do literally nothing until the empty response lands — and for the 44.0s build they do nothing except pollute the *next* turn’s context. The in-flight timer has zero causal contact with the failure you’re trying to catch.

The numbers:

Min productive latency = 5.5s > 5s threshold. The nudge fires on 100% of requests. It’s not a stall detector, it’s a per-turn tax.
The old 15s fired on 35.6 and 44.0 — i.e., it systematically penalized your *longest, most complex* generations (the build).
The killer constraint: idle (35.6s) < productive (44.0s). No threshold T separates them. Elapsed time carries no information about stall-vs-slow; the discriminating signal is in the response itself (finish=stop && tool_calls=[]), which arrives at 35.6s with zero false positives on the 44s case — no threshold tuning needed.
n=5. You’re tuning against the min of a five-sample distribution; even 6s wouldn’t clear it robustly.

Also: your observed “drift to unrelated tools” is probably caused by the nudge, not despite it. “Call a tool now” is content-free urgency. By recency, the model obeys the newest instruction — any tool, now — over its older plan. The 6.5s hallucinated collect_items (not in schema) is the same failure under pressure: hurry → schema hallucination → rejection → still zero executed tools → more nudges. Closed loop. The 15s detector already demonstrated it; 5s just spins the loop faster. If your nudge mechanism is cancel-and-resend rather than queue-for-next-turn, it’s worse — you’d abort the 44s build at 5s. (Specify which; the review differs.)

Fix: detect on response arrival, deterministically: finish=stop && tool_calls=[] && mode==task → that is the 35.6s case. Keep a time-based check only as a transport backstop (hung connection), at P99×3 or ~120s hard cap, handled as cancel-and-retry, not nudge.

2) False positives and guards
In-flight generation — all four productive samples. Guard: pause the timer while a request is in flight. A no-tool timer is only meaningful when nothing is in flight and nothing is executing.
Long-running tool execution — pathfinding, building, smelting routinely exceed 5s. If the counter resets on tool *completion* rather than issuance, you nudge mid-execution. Guard: reset on issuance.
Legitimate waiting — wait for day, mob despawn, crop growth. If there’s no wait/noop primitive, the nudge makes “correctly do nothing” impossible and converts patience into random action. Guard: an explicit wait(duration, reason) tool that resets the counter.
Conversational turns — this is a companion. finish=stop with no tools is correct behavior while answering a player. Guard: arm the detector only in task-execution mode.
Blocked on the planner — supervised architecture; waiting for approval/next subgoal means zero tool calls by design. Nudging then produces *unauthorized* action, which is strictly worse than stalling. Guard: only arm the timer when the companion is unblocked and expected to act.
Tool-rejection loops (the 6.5s case) — rejection is a schema/contract failure, not inattention. Routing it through the timer guarantees more pressure → more hallucinated tools. Guard: on rejection, immediately re-prompt with the actual tool list; classify as its own failure type.
Phase jitter — 1s polling × 5 checks = an effective 5–6s window depending on alignment; with a 0.5s margin (5 vs 5.5), phase decides firing. Fragile by construction.

Cross-cutting: nudge content must reference the current subgoal, not “a tool, any tool,” and must offer a compliant non-action escape (“call the next tool for subgoal X, or reply BLOCKED with reason”) so urgency has a legitimate outlet. Rate-limit to one nudge per episode with cooldown — a 44s request currently collects 8.

3) When to escalate to a real stalled state

Principle: nudge = attentional failure the model can self-correct (your 5.5s case recovered on its own); state change = structural failure or demonstrated non-recovery. Trigger escalation on deterministic events, not elapsed time:

2+ consecutive empty responses in task mode after a delivered nudge → soft channel failed. One empty response might be “task complete” — route that to the planner for adjudication instead of escalating.
N consecutive rejected tool calls → contract failure; nudges can’t fix it. Escalate to schema re-sync / tool-registry reset.
Transport hang — no response past the hard cap, connection timeout → cancel and retry with backoff. Queued nudges are useless here.
World-state evidence — no position/inventory/block delta across checks while a world-changing task is active. This is the ground truth, fully decoupled from LLM latency: measure stalls in the world, not in the API. (Same mode-gating caveat: exclude dialogue/planning tasks that legitimately don’t move the world.)

And note the architecture point: you already have a planner as the escalation target. The risk you’re avoiding — a 5s heuristic flipping task state — is real, but the fix is making the flip condition deterministic (response content, world deltas), not never flipping.

Bottom line: 15s→5s turns up the magnitude of a signal that carries no information. Move detection to response classification plus world deltas, and the threshold question dissolves.
